The FOMC’s October 2019 decision to cut the target range to 1.50–1.75% and to expand T-bill purchases/term and overnight repos to maintain ample reserves is consistent with evidence that monetary policy shocks have real short-run effects on output (Sims, 1992) and with sticky-price/wage frameworks where easing counteracts demand weakness (Christiano and Eichenbaum, 1992b). With inflation running below the symmetric 2% objective and expectations little changed, easing aligns with inflation-targeting guidance that emphasizes expectations management (Svensson). The Desk’s actions increase the monetary base to stabilize money markets and support transmission—an operational complement to the rate cut—without a regime shift. Credibility built since the Volcker era helps keep inflation expectations anchored, limiting risks from easing.

That said, ongoing weakness in business fixed investment and exports, plus dissent from two policymakers, signal uncertainty about the outlook. Strong labor markets versus below-target inflation yields a mildly positive but cautious tone overall.
